sections.overview: This Asian herbivore is native to the northern Indian subcontinent. Wild populations persist in scattered sites in India and Nepal, especially river floodplains. Its distribution reflects the link between grazing, abundant grass, water and seasonal wetlands.
sections.identification: Adult males can approach 2,200 kg and stand up to 2 m at the shoulder. Toronto Zoo lists male head-and-body length at 3.68–3.80 m and females at 3.10–3.40 m, with female mass around 1,600 kg; the broad figures vary with age and population. No reliable body-width measurement was found. Adults bear one dark nasal horn of compacted keratin, not bone. Thick grey-brown skin folds at the neck, shoulder and hindquarters, with raised bumps on the shoulders and upper legs. Its flexible upper lip gathers food; young rhinos develop adult folds as they mature.
sections.habitat: It favours low alluvial grasslands beside large rivers, with marshes, reed beds, pools and woodland. Flooding renews the plains, producing patches of tall grass and wet ground. Rhinos bathe and wallow, may move higher as floods rise, and also use dry grassland and forest edges.
sections.diet: Grasses, including tall riverine growth, form most of its diet. It also eats aquatic plants, leaves, shoots, twigs and fruit, varying its menu with season and vegetation. Its flexible upper lip gathers plants; it sometimes feeds partly submerged.
sections.behavior: Adults are usually solitary, though females stay with calves and animals may gather at grazing sites or wallows. Males hold loosely defended ranges and mark with dung and urine. Activity often peaks in cooler hours. Bathing and wallowing help with heat and biting insects; rhinos also rub against vegetation.
sections.reproduction: After about 15–16 months, a female gives birth to one calf. Breeding has no fixed annual season, and births are years apart. The calf soon walks and nurses; weaning takes about 12–18 months. Maternal care continues as it learns to forage and becomes independent.
sections.ecology: This large herbivore changes plant cover through grazing, trampling and paths. Dung returns seeds and nutrients to floodplain soil, and other wildlife uses its muddy wallows. These effects vary with local conditions.
sections.conservation: The IUCN’s 2019 Red List assessment classified it as Vulnerable, estimating 2,100–2,200 mature animals in 11 subpopulations and noting habitat decline. This dated assessment is not a current census. The International Rhino Foundation later reported about 4,075 wild animals after recovery under protection in India and Nepal. Poaching, floodplain habitat loss and fragmentation, and conflict near crowded reserves remain concerns.
